newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties, press hope Blair more pro-EU.
newsitem.headline: German parties, press hope Blair more pro-EU.

text.p: Germany's strongly pro-European politicians and press on Friday welcomed Tony Blair's landslide British election victory and hoped it meant London would play a more cooperative role in the European Union.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl, speaking in Brunei during an Asian tour, said the poll showed Britons did not like anti-European polemics and anti-EU policies could not win votes anywhere.
Trying to glow with reflected glory, the Social Democrats (SPD) hailed Blair's win as the start of a trend they hope will return them to power next year after 16 years in opposition.
Editorial writers were scathing about the defeated Conservatives, whose Eurosceptical and sometimes anti-German campaign offended sensitivities here.
Despite their reluctance to give up their mark currency, most Germans see European integration as a lofty ideal and anti-EU sentiments as the slippery slope towards a dangerous nationalism.
"This is an overwhelming mandate for the new government," said Kohl, who appeared in one Conservative campaign poster as a pro-EU ventriloquist with Blair as a dummy on his knee.

"Voters did not like the anti-European rhetoric of the past few days and weeks and this should be a lesson for all those who want to win votes with anti-European polemics," Kohl told reporters travelling with him.
"I would welcome it if Labour were more friendly towards Europe than the Conservatives were," he said.

Kohl said Labour was cautious about Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) and added: "I'm sure the new government will see very quickly and very clearly that standing on the sidelines amid all the developments in Europe will not bring any advantages for Britain."

Gerhard Schroeder, a potential SPD challenger to Kohl next year, told German journalists travelling with him in the United States that Blair had shown fellow left-of-centre parties how to combine modern economic policies with social justice.
SPD party manager Franz Muentefering said: "We say congratulations to the new prime minister and his party. We have decided to do the same in 74 weeks when the German election is held."
Television and radio programmes, noting the party had still not named its challenger to Kohl, promptly asked who was the "Tony Blair of the SPD."

Guenter Verheugen, the party's main foreign policy strategist, responded: "There's no sense asking who in Germany is like Tony Blair. Let's ask who the SPD in Germany can nominate and what he can learn from the methods, the style and comportment of Tony Blair.
"That applies to anyone who runs. Everyone can learn from that, no matter how old he is or how successful he has been in his life."
The liberal Frankfurter Rundschau daily said corruption and disputes over Europe had cost outgoing Prime Minister John Major his job.
"The conservative revolution that Margaret Thatcher began in 1979 has been stopped in 1997 after a political eternity," it said.

Berlin's Tagesspiegel hoped for a new beginning under New Labour, but said Blair had not been clear enough on his policies to know what to expect. "We will only be able to see something really new when he is actually in office."

Ruprecht Polenz, a deputy from Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and member of the German-British parliamentarians' group, said Blair's overwhelming majority could allow him to open up more towards Europe than he might have done with a narrower popular base.
Although it would probably be too late to join EMU at its launch in 1999, Britain could cooperate more at the intergovernmental conference updating the Maastricht treaties.
Polenz said the anti-German tone some Tories struck in their campaign had been irritating, especially when fanned by the tabloid press. But he added, "The election result showed it didnt't pay off.
